Lessons

The site's backing band plays every example in these lessons. Choose an instrument, a topic, or both. They run roughly from simpler to more involved.

No lessons match these choices yet.

  • Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

    Starting from the melody: hitting the change in bar 5, the blues and pentatonic scales, and a scale for each chord. Scales are shown as tablature, keyboard fingerings or a violin fingerboard, whichever you play.

  • Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

    For any instrument that plays one note at a time. Roots, chord tones, guide-tone lines, a riff, and the melody of Blues in the Closet, written in your own key.

  • Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

    What the chords of a blues are and how players vary them, from three chords to a jazz blues, with a chorus you can build yourself and an ear test.

  • Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

    Roots, then root and fifth, then the chord tones as a written line, then walking. Fretboard diagrams, bass-clef notation and the band's own bass line written out.

  • Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

    Two- and three-note chords built from the 3rd and 7th, on strings 5 and 4 and on strings 4 and 3, with the same shapes a tritone higher. No barre chords.

  • Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

    Left-hand roots, guide tones in the right hand, three-note shells and rootless left-hand voicings, each on a keyboard diagram and a grand staff.

  • Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

    The two great left hands of early jazz piano, played on the band one at a time, side by side on a blues, and swapped: stride leaps between bass and chord, boogie-woogie walks in eighths.

  • Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

    How to read a drum part, then the beat, the ride pattern, swing time, fills that mark the form, the shuffle, the slow 12/8 and straight eighths.

  • Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

    Why swing eighths are written as plain eighths, how far the long-short can stretch with tempo and style, and the range of good readings, with Blues in the Closet swung and Watermelon Man straight for contrast. Every example plays, with a swing slider.

  • Is Watermelon Man a Blues?

    Whether Herbie Hancock's Watermelon Man is a blues: its 16-bar form, its dominant-seventh chords, and what the site's "(Blues)" label means.

  • Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

    For a drummer who can already play a basic beat. The three sounds of the hi-hat, then quarter notes, eighths, accents, off-beats, an open note, open off-beats, sixteenths with one hand and with two, the foot alone and the swing hi-hat.

  • How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

    The drums, how to sit, the five strokes (bass, open, muted, slap, heel-toe) and how they are written, then the tumbao built in six steps with the band: open tones, right hand, left hand, both hands, a cha-cha band and two drums.

  • Watermelon Man for Congas

    The tumbao over a 16-bar blues: the form, the break on bar 14, the melody, and the same part in Mongo Santamar&iacute;a's cha-cha and in a boogaloo.

  • Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

    Matched grip (German, American, French) and traditional grip, fulcrum, rebound and the Moeller whip; then the other places kit players part ways: kit layout, left-handed and open-handed playing, throne height, pedal heel up or down, stick choice, and counting.

  • Playing Brushes

    What brushes are, how to hold them, sweeps against taps, the circle and the half-moon patterns for ballads and swing, the ride on a brush, and when to use them.

  • How to Play Cajón

    The Peruvian box drum: how to sit, the bass and slap tones, ghost notes, a basic rock and pop beat, a 6/8 feel, the Afro-Peruvian landó, and using brushes and extras.

  • First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

    G, D, Em, C for a whole class at once. Drums, bass, guitar, keyboard and voice each have four levels, from a first day on the instrument to a rock beat, root eighths and a folk-rock strum. The band plays the level you pick.

  • Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

    The four chords under most pop songs, made richer one move at a time: extensions, passing chords, secondary dominants and ii-V-Is. With a chorus you can build yourself and an ear test.

  • Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

    The C, Am, F, G changes as fretboard diagrams: open shapes, extensions, passing chords and secondary dominants.

  • Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

    The C, Am, F, G changes with a left-hand root and a right-hand chord, on a keyboard diagram and a grand staff.

  • Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

    The root of each chord, then the stepwise walking line through the passing chords, in bass clef and on a fretboard.

  • Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

    Thirteen steps from open triads and power chords through barre chords, 7ths, shells and top-string triads to drop 2, drop 3 and altered dominants, each with diagrams, a staff and sound.

  • Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

    The same chords ordered by what the fretting hand finds hard, from one-finger shapes to barres, muted strings and stretches, with what goes wrong at each step.

  • Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar

    From one finger on one string to trills, licks and the Sus embellishment on open D, A and C, each written in notation and tablature that plays.

  • Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

    Why a beginner tunes by ear from day one: matching a reference pitch, hearing beats (the wobble two nearly-equal notes make), tuning up to the note, and tuning against a drone. Strengths and weaknesses of each.

  • Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves

    Tuning the guitar to itself: the fifth-fret method, the harmonics method (and why its pure fourths are 2 cents off, and the G-to-B harmonic is 14 cents off), octave checks, and the final chord check. What each gets right and wrong.

  • Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits

    Needle, clip-on and strobe tuners: how they hear a note, why the reading jumps at the attack, why a guitar in tune on a tuner can still sound out (intonation, finger pressure, old strings), and how to use a tuner without letting it replace your ear.

  • String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

    Half-step, whole-step and 1½-step bends, curls, pre-bends, unison and double-stop bends, how they're written in tab, and the blue notes they reach in the A minor pentatonic box, with a drone to bend against.

  • Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

    Natural harmonics at the 12th, 7th, 5th, 4th/9th and 3rd frets and why they are there, how to touch and lift, tapped and harp harmonics, pinch harmonics with gain, bends and vibrato, how harmonics are written, faults and fixes, and a practice plan.

  • Travis Picking on Guitar

    The thumb alone, pinches, fingers between the thumb notes, then C, G, Am and D, chord changes, hammer-ons and pull-offs, and the band. Ends with a note on chicken pickin'.

  • Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

    Thirteen steps from triads and inversions through slash chords, 7ths, guide tones and shells to rootless, drop 2, spread, quartal and upper-structure voicings.

  • Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

    The same voicings ordered by what the hands find hard: span, black keys, two hands together, leaps, stretches and independence.

  • Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

    Major and minor triads with the root, 3rd or 5th in the bass, their figured-bass names (<span class="fb one"><span>6</span></span> and <span class="fb"><span>6</span><span>4</span></span>) and slash-chord names (C/E, C/G), on piano and guitar.

  • Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

    Breath, onsets, speech-level singing and the mix, words, safe belting, pentatonic runs, cry and flips, phrasing with a mic, and singing a third above. Exercises move into your range.

  • Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

    Conversational tone, swing eighths and ghost notes, scat syllables, the blues scale, arpeggios and guide tones through a ii-V-I, back-phrasing a ballad, and trading fours.

  • Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

    Appoggio breathing, onset and legato, the five Italian vowels, resonance, registers and the passaggio, the nine-note scale, messa di voce, vibrato, diction and solfège.

  • Formants: What Makes a Vowel

    What makes one vowel sound different from another: F1 and F2, the third formant, the singer's formant and formant tuning, heard on a synthesised voice.

  • Lesson: Four-Chord Loops

    The loops under a great many songs (I V vi IV, vi IV I V, the fifties loop, the turnaround, a borrowed chord, two minor loops) one at a time, each on a chart and a staff, with a loop builder and an ear test.

  • Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

    Authentic, half, deceptive, plagal and backdoor endings, each as a four-bar phrase on a staff, with the argument for why the plagal "Amen" is not a cadence, a phrase builder and two ear tests.

  • Lesson: Write an Ending

    The tune library's Unfinished Songs stop two bars short over V and I. Write the melody that ends them, in the Notation page, and hear it with the chords.

  • Lesson: Guide Tones

    The 3rd and 7th of each chord written as a single line over four-chord loops, a two-five-one and the turnaround. The band plays the line.

  • Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

    From natural-minor i, iv, v to the harmonic-minor V7, the Picardy third, a walking bass and the ii&deg;-V-i, in A minor.

  • Lesson: Borrowed Chords

    The minor iv, the &#9837;VII and the &#9837;VI borrowed into a major key, one at a time, with a chord-by-chord builder and an ear test.

  • Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes

    I-vi-ii-V made richer: sevenths, a dominant on the vi, starting on the iii, tritone substitutions and the first four bars of I Got Rhythm.

  • Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody

    One tune, Ode to Joy, with four sets of chords under it, played with the melody. Mix the settings two bars at a time.

  • Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

    The four jobs in a rhythm section, built up one player at a time. Switch players in and out while the band plays and see each part written out.

  • Arranging 2: Bass and Drums

    Why the bass follows the kick, how the groove sets the feel, walking in swing and the tumbao in Latin music.

  • Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards

    Comping: strum patterns, voicing and register, the off-beat chop, jazz comping, and two chord players without a fight.

  • Arranging 4: The Organ

    A playable tonewheel organ: pull the nine tonebars, switch the chorus, work the swell pedal and spin the Leslie, then hear it in the band.

  • Accompaniment Patterns

    A lesson for every bass line, comping rhythm, drum groove and conga part the band plays, each built up from simpler ones, played on the band and written out.

  • Composing 1: Writing a Melody

    Shape, steps and leaps, a climax, rhythm that repeats, and two classic eight-bar plans (the period and the sentence), each heard on the staff, then a melody of your own in the Notation page.

  • Composing 2: Developing a Motif

    A motif is a short idea that a piece keeps coming back to. Repetition, sequence, inversion, retrograde, augmentation, diminution and fragmentation, each heard, and a motif lab that builds a phrase from your own idea, one change at a time.

  • Composing 3: Words and Music

    Writing a song: putting stressed syllables on strong beats (prosody), rhyme and line length, verse, pre-chorus, chorus and bridge, the hook, and making the chorus sound different from the verse.

  • Composing 4: Instruments, Ranges and Transposing

    The orchestra's families, each instrument's lowest and highest notes, clefs, and transposing instruments (clarinet, trumpet, horn, saxophones), with a transposer that writes the part a player reads and checks it fits the instrument.

  • Composing 5: Arranging for Orchestra

    Melody, bass, harmony and countermelody: the four jobs in any arrangement, given to string quartet two ways, with doubling, spacing, passing the tune around, balance and rests, and a checklist for your own arrangement.

  • Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal

    Documenting how a piece was made: what to capture (ideas, versions, tests, feedback, decisions and reasons), recordings named so they can be found, annotated screenshots and scores, a weak entry next to a strong one, and an entry builder.

  • Process 2: MYP Criterion B, Developing (Grades 6–10)

    What MYP Arts Criterion B asks of a music student: practical exploration of ideas, and a clear artistic intention linked to the statement of inquiry, with choices stated, described, explained or justified. Ways to explore in sound, a sorting exercise, and an intention builder.

  • Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

    One melody as staff notation, jianpu, Hindustani and Carnatic sargam, a DAW piano roll and arrangement, a waveform and a spectrogram: what each shows, what it hides, and when to use it. With MYP and DP notes.

  • Score Reading 1: Alto and Tenor Clefs

    The movable C clef: alto clef for viola, tenor clef for cello, bassoon and trombone, why they exist, two quick ways to read them, and note-naming drills.

  • Score Reading 2: Instruments with Several Clefs

    Which instruments switch clefs and when: cello, bassoon, trombone, viola, double bass, horn, bass clarinet, keyboards and harp, plus the old octave conventions that still catch readers out.

  • Score Reading 3: Transposing Instruments

    What 'clarinet in B♭' means, how far each instrument transposes, how key signatures move, octave transpositions, and the difference between transposed and concert-pitch scores.

  • Score Reading 4: Why Transpositions Exist, and Horns in Every Key

    Natural horns and trumpets, crooks, valves, clarinets in B♭ and A, Sax's matched families and brass-band treble clef: why transposing parts exist, and how to read horn and trumpet parts in any key.

  • Score Reading 5: Strange Names (BB♭ Tuba and Friends)

    BB♭ and CC tubas, E♭ bass, tenor horn or alto horn, cor anglais, basso and alto, and the German, French and Italian names in scores (B means B♭, H means B).

  • Score Reading 6: Practice

    Drills and short score excerpts for everything in the series: note naming in four clefs, sounding pitches, key signatures both ways, horn in any key, and reading chords from a transposed score.

  • Ornaments by Period

    The same trill or small note means different things in Baroque, Classical, Romantic, 20th and 21st-century, and jazz scores. Hear each reading, with right and wrong interpretations for every period, how improvisation fits in then and now, and a flow chart for any ornament you meet.

  • Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

    Naming the parts of a song when you map a recording in Timestamp Notes: words or letters, solos, repeats, and how choruses are counted for each soloist.

  • Sources 1: Where Did You Find That? (Grades 6–8)

    For grades 6–8: what a source is, how to tell a good one from a weak one, why a Google AI summary is not a source, and how to write down where you found something.

  • Sources 2: Checking and Citing (Grades 9–10)

    For grades 9–10: primary and secondary sources in music, checking a source by reading around it (SIFT), why AI search answers can't be cited, and MLA citations for recordings, scores and web pages.

  • Sources 3: Research for DP Music (Grades 11–12)

    For IB DP Music: what examiners have said about research and evidence, especially in Exploring Music in Context: purposeful findings, primary and secondary sources, in-text references, timestamps, MuseScore, and why AI summaries are never evidence.

  • Annotated Bibliography 1: What It Is and Why I Chose It (Grades 6–8)

    For grades 6–8: what an annotated bibliography is, and a three-sentence recipe for each source (what it is, why you trust it, how you'll use it), with music examples.

  • Annotated Bibliography 2: Summarise, Evaluate, Connect (Grades 9–10)

    For grades 9–10: descriptive and evaluative annotations, MLA's format for an annotated bibliography, paraphrasing without copying, and judging sources against each other.

  • Annotated Bibliography 3: DP Music (Grades 11–12)

    For IB DP Music: the annotated bibliographies for Exploring, Experimenting as a Performer and the Collaborative Musical Project, what each must include, model annotations in MLA, and how they feed the final submission.

  • Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

    Why a pure major third does not beat and the piano's does, the syntonic and Pythagorean commas, and what twelve equal steps cost. Hear both on sine waves, the drone and a chord keyboard, then meet meantone, well temperaments and tunings that are not twelve-note.

  • How a Strobe Tuner Works

    The spinning disc and flashing lamp of the Strobotuner, why a pattern stands still (the wagon-wheel effect), one band for each partial, the multiply-and-average arithmetic of the software version, drift as beat rate and cents, stiff strings and weak fundamentals, and just against equal temperament. Watch it follow the page's own sound, no microphone.

  • Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

    Why some partials are not whole-number multiples: string stiffness (with a calculator), old strings, mode locking, brass and clarinet, formants, marimba and xylophone bars, chimes, church bells, timpani and gamelan. What a player can change (levels, not pitch) and what only the maker can, with every instrument as a practice preset on the strobe tuner.

  • Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier

    The harmonics of a note written out over any root, with how far each is from the piano. Build square, triangle, sawtooth and pulse waves from sine waves.

  • Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation

    The classic synth waves on an oscilloscope and spectrum, pulse width, and PWM.

  • Sound 3: Noise

    White, pink and brown noise, and wind, surf, hi-hats, snares and rain made from it.

  • Sound 4: Filters

    Low-pass, high-pass, resonance, band-pass, notch and EQ, on noise, music or your own voice.

  • Sound 5: Envelopes

    Attack, decay, sustain and release: why a piano, an organ and a violin playing the same note sound different.

  • Sound 6: LFOs

    Vibrato, tremolo, wah and auto-pan from one slow oscillator, and what happens when it speeds up.

  • Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis

    A two-oscillator synth with filter, envelopes and LFO, played from the keys or MIDI, with presets for bass, brass, pads and plucks.

  • Sound 8: FM Synthesis

    Carrier, modulator, ratio and index: sidebands on the spectrum, and bells, electric piano and bass from two sine waves.

  • Sound 9: Wavetable Synthesis

    Morph through a table of wave shapes by hand or with an LFO.

  • Sound 10: Granular Synthesis

    A sound cut into hundreds of grains: freeze it, stretch it without changing its pitch, or scatter it into a cloud. Record your own voice.

  • Sound 11: The Equaliser

    High-pass, shelves and bells, what lives in each frequency range, cut before you boost, and finding a hidden ringing frequency by ear.

  • Sound 12: Distortion

    Overdrive, distortion and fuzz told apart; soft clip, hard clip, tube-like, wavefolder and bit crusher, and the harmonics each one adds.

  • Sound 13: The Compressor

    Threshold, ratio, knee, attack and release, with a live gain-reduction meter.

  • Sound 14: Sidechain

    Music ducking under a kick drum, from invisible glue to EDM pumping, and radio-style ducking under a voice.

  • Sound 15: Gates and Transients

    A noise gate, the 80s gated-reverb snare, and a transient shaper for punch or room.

  • Sound 16: Reverb

    A convolution reverb with a room you build: decay, pre-delay, damping and early reflections; spring reverb, shimmer and freeze.

  • Sound 17: Delay

    Slapback, tempo echoes, ping-pong, tape and dub feedback, and a glitch stutter that loops slices of the beat.

  • Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger

    Moving short delays, the Doppler effect, and the comb filter.

  • Sound 19: Phaser

    All-pass filters, phase and sweeping notches.

  • Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker

    Tremolo, auto-pan, and a spinning Leslie speaker with its horn and drum speeding up at different rates.
